title: A Parasite Makes Ants Climb Grass at Night and Wait to Be Eaten

scenes.text: These ants climb grass at night and wait to be eaten.
They clamp their jaws on the tip and freeze till dawn. Something is driving them.
scenes.keywords: ant on grass tip close up

scenes.text: Hundreds of liver fluke larvae ride inside each ant. One sits in its brain.
At about eight degrees, that larva makes the ant climb and lock on.
Past thirty-six degrees, the ant lets go and walks home like nothing happened.
The fluke only grows up inside a grazing cow or deer. So it parks its ant where the mouths are.

description:
Ants infected with the lancet liver fluke climb grass blades and clamp on with their jaws, waiting to be swallowed by a grazing animal.
A 2023 University of Copenhagen study tracked 1,264 infected wood ants in a Danish forest: hundreds of fluke larvae sit in each ant, one lodges in its brain, and temperature decides everything. Cool mornings and evenings, the ants climb and bite down; in the heat of the day they let go and go back to normal, then do it all again at dusk.
The fluke needs a cow, sheep or deer to finish its life cycle, and a snail before the ant.
Which parasite trick creeps you out the most?
thumbnail_text: ONE LARVA. IN THE ANT'S BRAIN

first_comment: The fluke's full route: snail, then ant, then cow or deer. The ant eats the snail's slime balls to catch it. Which parasite trick creeps you out the most?
